blocks.text: For its 83rd issue, the 100 Photos for Press Freedom collection takes life from the Doisneau side. More than yet another tribute to the great master, this volume was conceived as a joyfully committed guide to inhabiting the world differently.

There are times that make you want to close your eyes. Ours has no shortage of reasons to. So we went digging into the world of Robert Doisneau. Not out of nostalgia, but because his work reminds us of something essential: it is still possible to look at the world without letting its brutality contaminate us.

His photographs, which have become icons and have been reproduced endlessly, have at times ended up masking the diversity and modernity of his work. The images gathered in this book reveal a gaze that is tender and funny, but also free, defiant, attentive to the margins, to gestures of resistance, and to those who refuse to march in step.
Through six chapters, conceived as so many invitations to live differently, RSF offers a chance to rediscover a body of work we thought we knew.

Slow down, first, in the manner of a man who described himself as less a hunter than a “fisher of images,” and who knew how to let time and chance do their work. Celebrate, next, in the village dance halls and bistros where bodies let loose, where festivity thumbs its nose at the seriousness of the world. Disobey, because living Doisneau-style also means preferring the side roads. Resist, in the face of the world’s brutality, without ever giving up one’s freedom. Look, truly, with enough attention to spot the tiny detail that suddenly tips the banal into the marvelous. And finally, love: one’s friends, one’s loved ones, one’s companions along the way.
What is this album for?

Looking at Doisneau’s photographs, but also at his life, his friendships and his commitments, a philosophy emerges: look elsewhere, take a step to the side, stay curious, free and deeply connected to others.
With this new album, Reporters Without Borders offers you a manual for a better life, for standing tall and joyful in the world.
The portfolio of about a hundred pages opens with a foreword by David Castello-Lopes, accompanied by new, illuminating texts by Patrice Leconte, Marie Desplechin and Clémentine Deroudille.
10 Pages on Press Freedom and RSF’s Work
An unmissable fixture of the collection, the final section puts into words and images the album’s primary function: funding RSF’s fight for press freedom around the world.
Who Has It In for Press Freedom?
Intimidation, violence, cyberharassment, arrests: attacks on the press take many forms around the world. Portraits of four of the thirty-six predators of press freedom identified by RSF in 2026.
Benjamin Netanyahu, Mediacide Alert

Over two decades, “Bibi” will have severely undermined press freedom and the very existence of the press: in Gaza, closed to foreign media, where his army has killed dozens of bona fide journalists; in the West Bank, where Israeli settlers hunt reporters with impunity; in Israel, where independent newspapers and media are regularly vilified and attacked, and also hampered by laws designed to silence them.
Le Lynx, 34 Years of Satire

In Guinea, the paper stands as an exception. An independent satirical weekly, Le Lynx has stood out since 1992 for its incisive cartoons. Today, its main challenge is surviving amid the predation of the free and independent press.
Defenders of Press Freedom

RSF defends, around the world, those who stubbornly bear witness to the reality of the facts, all too often at the risk of their lives or their freedom. Discover the stories of Nataliia Sadykova, Doan Bao Chau and Julia Mengolini.
Doisneau, Tireless Devotee of Imperfection
Robert Doisneau was born on April 14, 1912, in Gentilly. At 15, he entered the École Estienne in Paris, where he learned the trade of lithographic engraver.
In 1931, he became an operator in the studio of photographer André Vigneau. There he discovered photography and the world of artistic creation.
In 1932, he sold his first photo-reportage to the daily newspaper L’Excelsior . His images were devoted to the Saint-Ouen flea market.

From 1934 to 1939, he worked as an industrial photographer at the Renault factories in Billancourt. He photographed the workshops, the workers and the assembly lines. In 1939, he was fired for repeated lateness and became a freelance photographer.
During the Second World War, his photographic projects were interrupted. He put his engraving skills at the service of the Resistance by forging identity papers.
In 1946, he joined the Rapho agency.

In 1949, he published his first book with the writer Blaise Cendrars, La Banlieue de Paris , devoted to a territory that would remain at the heart of his work. The same year, he became a contributor to Vogue magazine.
In 1950, he made Le Baiser de l’hôtel de ville (The Kiss at the Hôtel de Ville), which would become one of his most famous photographs and one of the emblematic images of postwar Paris.

In 1983, Robert Doisneau received the Grand Prix national de la photographie. The following year, he took part in the DATAR Photographic Mission and returned to the Paris suburbs, which he this time photographed in color.
On April 1, 1994, Robert Doisneau died in Paris at the age of 81. He left behind nearly 450,000 negatives.

Founded in 1985, Reporters Without Borders (RSF) works for the freedom, independence and pluralism of journalism across the planet. Holding consultative status at the UN and UNESCO, the Paris-based organization has 14 bureaus and sections and more than 150 correspondents around the world. It provides concrete support to journalists in the field through mobilization campaigns, legal and material assistance, and physical and digital security systems and tools. The organization is an essential interlocutor for governments and international institutions, and each year publishes the World Press Freedom Index, which has become a reference tool.

The sale of the photo albums is an essential resource for Reporters Without Borders. Thanks to the support of its partners: France Messagerie, the SNDP, Culture Presse, the Maisons de la Presse, Mag Presse, Mediakiosk, Promap, Relay, Interforum, Fnac, as well as all the retailers that distribute the album free of charge, the profits from these sales are paid in full to the association.
